turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on in, I'll grab a set of vitals before the doctor. Pop this under your tongue.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok. Uh, sorry, I'm kind of shaky.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Temp is 100.2 fahrenheit. Blood pressure one twenty eight over seventy eight, pulse 92, oxygen sat 98 percent. You're alright to sit.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): My sister had a crown last spring and she was totally fine, but my little guy is teething molars this week so nobody at my house is sleeping.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hi, I'm Dr. Shah. Tell me what's going on.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): My right cheek swelled up and the tooth under the new crown is throbbing. It's been, err, three days. I couldn't get my dentist, he's out till next week.
[SEG0007] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's been a wreck. The pain shoots into her ear, she can barely open her mouth, and she hasn't eaten anything.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Dan, the ear is fine, it does not go into my ear. I can open my mouth, just not all the way. And I had soup last night, I'm just scared to chew on that side.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Alright. So the cheek and the tooth, not the ear, at least not yet. When was the crown put on?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Uh, five days ago. The throb started the next day, so about four days of toothache, and the cheek puffiness is three days. It hurts more when I bite down.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever at home, chills?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I felt warm, kind of mild. I never actually checked a number. No chills.
[SEG0013] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She felt burning hot last night. I thought it was 102.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Nobody took it, Dan. I was just warm, not, um, not burning up.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Trouble swallowing? Shortness of breath? Any feeling the throat is closing?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Swallowing's ok. Breathing is, um, normal. That's the part I'm scared of, that it spreads there.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, cough, stiff neck?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of those.

[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me look. Right cheek is swollen, warm, tender to touch. Gum around the lower right crown is red and puffy. I don't see pus. Mouth opening is about two fingers, so limited, not locked shut.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Is two fingers bad? Am I gonna lose the tooth? Could this be sepsis? How fast can it get dangerous?

[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking this is a dental abscess under that crown. The swelling is your body fighting the infection, fluid and immune cells packing into the cheek. I don't see sepsis. The dentist has to say if the tooth can be saved.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok. Ok. So what do I do if he can't see me till next week? Do I just wait?
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): We don't wait on the infection. Any drug allergies? Penicillin, sulfa, anything?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing.
[SEG0025] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Didn't you get a rash from a sulfa pill though?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): That was my brother, not me. I've never taken sulfa. Err, no allergies, I promise.
[SEG0027] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Right, yeah, that was him. Sorry.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): What are you taking now?

[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Ibuprofen, four hundred milligrams, about every six hours for four days, for the tooth. The dentist gave me amoxicilin, five hundred milligrams, I took one capsule and then I stopped it, my stomach turned. He also wrote a Medrol pack, the steroid, but I never picked it up, never took a single one.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): One dose of amoxicillin and you stopped. Was it a rash, swelling, or just the stomach?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Just nausea. No rash. It settled after I quit. I didn't take another one.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Can I keep the ibuprofen with whatever you give me? Will an antibiotic even work with the crown still on? How long till the swelling goes down?

[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, keep the ibuprofen, take it with a little food. It helps the pain and some of the inflammation. I'm starting clindamycin, three hundred milligrams by mouth, three times a day, for seven days, because the amoxicillin bothered your stomach. Finish the whole course.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Three times a day for seven days? What if I miss a dose? I read clindamycin can wreck your gut. Is that true? Should I take a probiotic?

[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Space them as evenly as you can, and if you miss one just take the next when it's due, don't double. If you get bad watery diarrhea, stop and call, that can happen with this drug, and a probiotic isn't required. Bigger thing, if swallowing gets hard, if breathing changes, or the swelling climbs toward the eye or down into the neck, go to the ER, don't sit on that.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Toward the eye? Like, how much swelling is too much? Should I check a mirror every hour? I'm going to obsess.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Once or twice a day is enough, not every hour. A little more puffiness the first day can happen. A jump in size, or you can't swallow your spit, that's the ER.

[SEG0038] person_1 (NURSE): I can send the script and the instructions to the pharmacy on file. My sister's abscess ended up needing a root canal, so sometimes the tooth still needs work later. Not trying to scare you.
[SEG0039] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Should she call out of work?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I shelve books at the library, part time. I was gonna go in tomorrow. Is that stupid?

[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Rest tomorrow. Soft foods, chew on the other side. Library can wait a couple days till the pain eases. I want to see you back here in two days to recheck this swelling, whether it feels better or not, and call the dentist the morning they're open.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Even if I feel fine in two days? And if the clindamycin makes me sick like the amoxicillin did, do I stop or push through?

[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come in at two days either way, I'll look. Mild nausea, take it with food and keep going. If you vomit the doses or a rash shows up, call us and we'll change it. No blood tests today, the fever's mild and your airway is clear.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. Alright. I still feel kind of panicky but that helps.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): You came in at the right time. We'll get that prescription moving.

spec.situation: Cheek swelling and throbbing toothache for three days after a crown; fever mild; dentist unavailable; doctor prescribes antibiotic, warns about swallowing or breathing difficulty.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

features: relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

bad.reason: Dose, one dose, and discontinued supported; indication was not explicitly stated as tooth pain.
bad.text: amoxicillin (dose=500 mg, frequency=single dose, duration=1 dose, indication=tooth pain, status=discontinued, reported_by=patient)

bad.reason: Airway clear is stated, but not as a direct physical exam finding by doctor at exam.

omissions.text: Family member said the patient 'hasn't eaten anything,' but the patient corrected this: she had soup last night and is afraid to chew on that side rather than unable to eat.
Negative finding asked and answered but not recorded: no feeling that the throat is closing.
Examination detail not recorded: mouth opening was limited but 'not locked shut.'
Assessment detail not recorded: doctor stated 'I don't see sepsis.'
Medication history not recorded: a Medrol pack (steroid) had been prescribed by the dentist, but the patient never picked it up and never took any doses.
Reason amoxicillin was stopped should be recorded more specifically as stomach upset/nausea rather than allergy; doctor confirmed there was no rash or swelling, only nausea.
Return precaution not recorded: go to the ER if unable to swallow saliva/spit.
Plan detail not recorded: no blood tests were done today because the fever was mild and the airway was clear.
